passages.title: Price ladder — masstige gap (India)
passages.text: The observed India ladder is barbelled. Mass sits at Rs500-700 (India D2C serum), and imported K-beauty premium sits at Rs2000-2999 (Anua toner, large-format Innisfree). Between them, the Rs700-1600 masstige band is populated almost entirely by K-beauty SKUs that reach it only through heavy promotion — COSRX essence lists at Rs1490 MRP but sells at Rs969; Innisfree's small serum lands at Rs680 on Blinkit; The Face Show/Laneige/Etude q-commerce SKUs sit Rs600-1600. This is precisely the corridor's opening: mid-price derma K-beauty at a genuine (not promo-dependent) Rs700-1500 shelf price on the q-commerce rail into Tier 2/3 (baseline whitespace #5). The MRP-vs-promoted spread is the tell — brands are papering the masstige gap with discounts on premium-listed SKUs rather than pricing a true masstige tier, which an entrant with lower landed cost (e.g. India-manufactured Korean-ingredient line) could occupy directly.

passages.title: Risk — data-confidence (BOTH)
passages.text: Severity HIGH. Most India segment sizes and growth rates rest on LOW-confidence aggregators (IMARC, TechSci, Mordor, P&S, MarkWide, EMR) and carry unresolved definitional gaps: India dermocosmetics spans a ~7x range (P&S US$256m 2023 vs MarkWide US$1.85bn 2026), sun care shows a ~2.3x base gap, and hair-care CAGR reads split 4.73% vs 10.58%. Korea's core skincare/derma/men's figures are Euromonitor HIGH, but several KR segments are export-value-only. Building an entry case on these numbers risks anchoring to a figure that is definitional noise, not signal. Mitigation: Lean on the HIGH-confidence anchors (Euromonitor KR retail, UN Comtrade trade flows, Euromonitor IN men's grooming) and treat aggregator CAGRs as scenario ranges, not point estimates. Apply the repo's >20% reconciliation gap rule: where top-down and bottom-up diverge, find the definitional mismatch before publishing a number. Flag every value_basis_uncertain item in the entry case.

passages.title: Risk — concentration (BOTH)
passages.text: Severity MEDIUM. The market-share reads are shares of only 2-3 listed brand owners each (KR: LG H&H, AmorePacific; IN: HUL, Godrej, Honasa), computed on NET_REALISATION revenue, excluding all unorganised/unlisted players, and inflated by non-pure-play conglomerates carrying non-BPC revenue. They are coverage indicators, not true category shares. Reading 'competitive openness' or rivalry directly off them would overstate incumbent dominance and misjudge how contestable a segment actually is. Mitigation: Read shares as coverage indicators, never as market shares; do not net conglomerate revenue against BPC-only sizes. Where a competitive-openness judgment is needed, ground it in channel and assortment evidence (conduit portfolios, q-commerce depth) rather than these share tables.

passages.title: Risk — regulatory (IN) (India)
passages.text: Severity HIGH. Any imported cosmetic requires CDSCO import registration (Form COS-1 to COS-2 via SUGAM) as pre-clearance before any consignment, plus manufacturing-site registration and BIS IS 4707 compliance (Part 2 revised Aug 2025); paper filings are no longer accepted as of 2026. This gates the entire import_corridor thesis: no registration, no shipment. The severity is compounded because cost and timeline are not quantified anywhere in the current data. Mitigation: Budget CDSCO lead-time and working capital into any import_corridor plan and file registration well ahead of first shipment. Commission a regulatory pass (per the /regulatory backlog) to quantify COS-2 cost and timeline before committing volume. Where registration is a blocker, partner with a conduit that already holds registrations for the brand.

passages.title: Risk — FX pinning (BOTH)
passages.text: Severity MEDIUM. All USD normalisation is pinned to a single FX date (USD/KRW 1478.40, USD/INR 96.23, both 2026-07-21), and KR retail figures are converted via the inverse of that rate. Cross-geography comparisons and any KRW-cost / INR-revenue corridor margin are sensitive to rate drift away from that pin, so a comparison that looks clean today can move purely on FX. Mitigation: Re-pin FX each research pass and record the rate + date with every conversion; always show original currency alongside the USD equivalent; never net figures across value_basis, and flag corridor margin reads as FX-sensitive.

passages.title: Risk — single-source (BOTH)
passages.text: Severity MEDIUM. Several load-bearing figures rest on a single source with no triangulation: the corridor trade base (baseline report only), the q-commerce assortment picture (one Blinkit snapshot, 2026-07-23), the Nykaa K-beauty GMV growth (one earnings citation), the KR total market size (Euromonitor only) and the IN headline market size (Statista via China Briefing, value_basis uncertain). Any of these moving would shift the entry case, and none is currently corroborated. Mitigation: Triangulate each single-source figure with a second independent source before using it as load-bearing; re-run the q-commerce tracker on a schedule so the assortment read is a trend, not a one-off; keep value_basis_uncertain items explicitly labelled in the entry case.

passages.title: Route to market — e-commerce (India)
passages.text: India online BPC reached ~INR 56,000cr in FY26, growing ~35% YoY (Redseer, Habit or Desire); digital channels were ~9.4% of BPC revenue in 2025 (baseline, LOW); e-commerce is projected to reach 34-38% of ALL India BPC spend by 2030 (Redseer, Beauty Blitz 2030 — implying offline still holds ~62-66%). Beauty platforms Nykaa/Tira/Flipkart/Amazon are the K-beauty conduits: Nykaa runs the 10-year AmorePacific portfolio (Innisfree, Laneige, Sulwhasoo, COSRX, Aestura, Illiyoon) and now also carries independent K-brands (TirTir Jun-2026, Medicube); Reliance's Tira is on a 2026 exclusive-launch sprint (Hince Jan, Medicube Feb, Dr. Melaxin Jul). Platform commissions are steep — Nykaa 22-28% by category (skincare ~24%, colour ~26%; Sylvr); Amazon.in referral 7-10% above INR1,000 but 0% below INR1,000 effective Mar-2026 (KwickMetrics). Entry implication: The online rail is where a K-beauty entrant lands first: it is the fastest-growing channel and the established conduit for imported Korean SKUs, requiring no GT/MT distribution build. But platform economics are demanding — budget ~22-28% of sell-through to Nykaa, while Amazon's zero referral below INR1,000 tilts the maths toward entry-price hero SKUs. Conduit choice is a strategic fork: Nykaa's incumbent AmorePacific tie-up versus Tira's exclusive-launch land grab.

passages.title: Route to market — quick-commerce (India)
passages.text: Q-commerce is ~INR 40,000cr (~US$5bn) GMV in 2026, split roughly Blinkit 45-50% / Zepto 20-25% / Instamart 20-25% (Digital in Asia). BPC is the second-largest q-commerce category — ~8.5% of total q-commerce GMV in CY25, up from ~2.8% CY22; within online BPC, q-commerce rose to ~16% CY25 (from ~2% CY22) and ~18% FY26 (from 9% FY25) per Redseer. BPC GMV on q-commerce grew 120%+ YoY FY26 / ~140% CY25, and beauty on q-commerce +160% YoY (RedSeer via Unicommerce); BPC is ~13.4% of Blinkit's daily sales (Unicommerce). A live Blinkit capture (2026-07-23) shows the rail splits by ownership: conglomerate K-brands are deeply stocked (LG H&H's The Face Shop 21 SKUs, AmorePacific's Laneige 16 / Etude 10 / Innisfree 9), but the viral indie/derma brands driving the narrative are thin or absent (COSRX out-of-stock, Anua 'coming soon', Some By Mi / Isntree / Mixsoon absent). Take rates: Blinkit 18-22% base commission on MRP (~38% all-in incl. fulfilment/ads); Zepto ~22-23% (NewsBytes). Entry implication: Q-commerce is the access rail into Tier 2/3 and the corridor's clearest whitespace (baseline #5, mid-price derma K-beauty). The gap is not the conglomerate brands already on the shelf — it is getting indie/derma K-beauty onto dark-store slots. All-in economics (~38% on Blinkit) plus commission charged on MRP (not discounted price) mean an entrant must price for a high channel take. Dark-store SKU counts are small, so the play is a tight hero-SKU assortment, not a full range.

passages.title: Route to market — D2C (India)
passages.text: India's D2C beauty engine runs on third-party contract manufacturers (MOQs from ~500 units); the brand owns formula and brand, the CM owns production (Gorgeous Cosmos; hundreds on IndiaMART). Funding continues despite the broader D2C slowdown — ~US$757m into India D2C over 18 months (wellness+beauty led), with KOSE putting US$30m into Foxtale, Moxie raising US$15m and Antinorm an INR28cr seed (The D2C Pulse). D2C is projected to hold ~10% of online BPC by 2030 (Redseer). Indian D2C brands are already going Korean at local price points — Pilgrim's Korean Rice Water range, Limese (formulated in Korea for Indian skin), and Foxtale's Hula Hoop house-of-brands play (corridor.yaml india_side_players). Entry implication: A K-beauty entrant can side-step import registration entirely by building an India D2C line (own brand via contract manufacturer) — the Limese/Pilgrim template — trading corridor authenticity for speed, lower landed cost and no CDSCO COS-2 wait. Own-site D2C also escapes the 22-38% platform/q-commerce take, but must self-fund traffic. Deep contract-manufacturing capacity makes a made-in-India Korean-ingredient line feasible at mass Rs500-700 price points.

passages.title: Route to market — general trade (India)
passages.text: GT (kirana) still dominates Indian retail — offline is projected to retain ~62-66% of BPC even in 2030 (Redseer, Beauty Blitz 2030). Kirana margins run 5-10% on national brands with strong consumer pull but 18-25%+ demanded from NEW/unfamiliar brands; distributor all-in cost for smaller brands is 20-30% of sale price (Kirana Club). A Storewise worked example shows the structure — distributor/substockist ~12%, retailer ~20% on a mid-FMCG SKU. These are FMCG-wide benchmarks, not BPC-specific. Entry implication: GT is a heavy lift for an import-led K-beauty entrant: a new/unknown brand pays the top of the margin band (18-25%+ retailer, 20-30% distributor all-in) and needs a physical distributor network to reach kirana. It is not an entry channel — it is a scale channel to attempt only after online/q-commerce prove demand. Imported unit economics rarely survive GT margins stacked on top of CDSCO-landed cost.

passages.title: Route to market — modern trade (India)
passages.text: Modern-trade (organised chains, beauty specialty stores) evidence is thin — no modern-trade-specific BPC margin surfaced on any fetched page (explicitly noted in the trade-margin research). The nearest specialty-retail proxy is beauty platforms' own physical formats — Tira's select stores, used alongside online for K-beauty exclusive launches (corridor.yaml). Entry implication: research needed — insufficient standalone MT data to size the channel or its economics. For a K-beauty entrant, MT currently surfaces mainly as the physical arm of omnichannel platforms (Tira stores) rather than an independent route; treat it as an extension of the platform relationship until MT-specific data lands.

passages.title: Route to market summary (India)
passages.text: For a K-beauty entrant, India's route to market is online-first: e-commerce platforms (Nykaa/Tira/Flipkart/Amazon) are the proven conduit for imported Korean SKUs and the fastest-growing channel (~35% YoY), while quick-commerce (~US$5bn GMV, BPC growing 120-140% YoY) is the Tier 2/3 access rail and the corridor's clearest whitespace — specifically getting indie/derma K-beauty onto dark stores the conglomerate brands already occupy. Both online routes carry heavy take rates (Nykaa 22-28%, Blinkit ~38% all-in on MRP), so pricing must absorb the channel. D2C via contract manufacturing offers a CDSCO-free, lower-cost alternative at mass price points (the Limese/Pilgrim Korean-ingredient template). General trade is a post-proof scale channel where new brands pay punishing margins (18-30%), and modern trade lacks standalone data — research needed.

passages.title: Route to market — H&B stores (Olive Young) (South Korea)
passages.text: Health & beauty specialty stores are Korea's anchor beauty channel — Mordor puts them at ~54.1% of 2025 cosmetics distribution, led by CJ Olive Young, which holds MORE THAN 85% of the Korean H&B STORE market with 1,380+ stores (Seoulz). Olive Young standalone revenue was KRW 5.83tn (~US$4.2bn) in CY2025, +21.8% YoY (Seoulz); Daxue reports KRW 4.8tn consolidated 2024, +23.9% YoY. Notably, 26.4% of Olive Young's H1 2025 customers were foreign — tourist beauty spend is shifting out of duty-free and into H&B stores (Korea Times). Entry implication: Olive Young is the single most important shelf in Korea and a near-gatekeeper for domestic H&B distribution — winning it is close to winning the channel, but that dominance hands it strong buyer power over an entrant's terms and margins. Its rising foreign-customer share also makes it a discovery surface: a brand that proves out on Olive Young builds the reference to later travel the corridor to India.

passages.title: Route to market — online (e-commerce) (South Korea)
passages.text: Online is the largest channel by the Korea Ratings measure — 60.8% of the Korea cosmetics market in CY2024, up from 39.1% in 2019; Korea's online cosmetics transaction value was KRW 13.8tn (~US$9.25bn) in 2024, +7.7% YoY (Statistics Korea via press). This 60.8% online figure CONFLICTS with Mordor's 54.1% H&B-store share for 2025 — different channel definitions and coverage, so the two must not be added. Entry implication: E-commerce is either the largest or second-largest Korean channel depending on definition, and it grows steadily (~8% on online transaction value). For an entrant it is the lowest-barrier domestic route, but the definitional overlap with H&B means online and Olive Young should be treated as overlapping — not additive — when sizing reachable demand.

passages.title: Route to market — department store (South Korea)
passages.text: Department stores are the prestige tier of Korean beauty retail, but the available split combines them with drugstores: offline (department stores + drugstores) was 39.2% of the Korea cosmetics market in CY2024, down from 60.9% in 2019 (Korea Ratings) — a structural decline as online and H&B took share. The source does not break out a department-store-only figure. Entry implication: The prestige department-store channel is shrinking and is not separated out in the data, so it is a weak standalone entry route. It matters only for a premium-positioned brand; a masstige/derma K-beauty entrant should skip it in favour of H&B and online.

passages.title: Route to market — duty-free (distinct channel) (South Korea)
passages.text: Duty-free is a DISTINCT channel (repo rule 12 — never folded into domestic retail) and it is in structural decline: Korea duty-free sales were US$7.3bn Jan-Oct 2025, -16.6% YoY, headed for the lowest full year since 2015 (pre-pandemic >US$20bn/yr; AJU Press); KRW 6.36tn in H1 2025 (Korea Times). Figures cover all duty-free categories, not beauty only (cosmetics was historically the largest). The driver is the collapse of Chinese daigou/tourist buying, with the displaced tourist beauty spend migrating into Olive Young H&B stores. Entry implication: Duty-free is a declining, tourist-dependent channel an entrant should not build a Korea strategy around; its historic role as the daigou export back-door has broken down. Its decline is itself a signal — prioritise domestic H&B and online, where the displaced tourist demand is landing.

passages.title: Route to market summary (South Korea)
passages.text: Korea's beauty distribution splits between two dominant domestic channels whose measured shares conflict by definition: H&B specialty stores (~54% per Mordor, anchored by Olive Young at >85% of the H&B store market and KRW 5.83tn revenue) and online (~61% per Korea Ratings, KRW 13.8tn transaction value) — the two overlap and must not be summed. For an entrant, Olive Young is the near-gatekeeper shelf and online the lowest-barrier route; both are also where displaced tourist demand is concentrating. Department stores are a shrinking prestige tier (only available combined with drugstores, ~39% offline) relevant to premium brands only. Duty-free is a distinct, structurally declining channel (US$7.3bn Jan-Oct 2025, -16.6% YoY) hollowed out by the daigou collapse — flagged separately and not to be built around.

passages.title: Value Chain — operating margins
passages.text: India brand-owner operating margins fan out sharply by model: legacy FMCG runs highest (Hindustan Unilever ~23%, Godrej Consumer ~21% FY26), the D2C challenger sits far lower (Honasa ~10%), and the pure retailer thinnest of all (Nykaa/FSN ~8%). The spread says the profit pool concentrates at scale-manufacturing incumbents; a new brand entering as a D2C or riding a retail platform should underwrite low-double-digit or single-digit operating margins, not FMCG-grade economics, at least until it earns scale.

passages.title: Value Chain — gross/trade margins
passages.text: Category gross margins are wide but heavily eroded downstream. A 30ml serum shows a 75-85% gross markup (COGS Rs80-120 vs MRP Rs500-700), yet the D2C Pulse itself flags that true margin falls sharply after packaging, shipping and returns. On the platform side, Nykaa takes roughly a 22-26% commission on skincare brands (~24% midpoint), higher for new brands. The headline gross margin is real but is not the margin an entrant keeps: platform commission plus fulfilment is the binding economic reality.

passages.title: Value Chain — import dependence
passages.text: India skincare is ~91% domestically supplied by value (imports ~US$844m against a ~US$9bn market), with imports concentrated in the premium and K-beauty tiers — Korea ~17% and China ~22% of skincare imports. HS 3304 imports from Korea were US$140m in 2024 (Comtrade, HIGH). Premium fragrance is the exception (import-reliant, UAE/France-led; ~12.8% dependence), while mass perfume/deodorant is domestically filled. The read for a Korean entrant: you are competing in the ~9% import slice, not the whole market, and that slice is exactly where the corridor pull sits.

passages.title: Value Chain — contract manufacturing
passages.text: Most Indian D2C beauty brands own formula and brand but not factories — they run on third-party contract manufacturers / private-label houses (Gorgeous Cosmos and hundreds on IndiaMART) with MOQs from ~500 units. Two service models coexist: FMCG buyers demand audit-readiness and scale, D2C buyers demand agility, small batches and RM transparency. Upstream, Galaxy Surfactants (mild surfactants) and Fine Organics (specialty additives) anchor domestic actives supply. The implication is a genuinely low build barrier — an entrant can launch a domestic-made brand without capex — but differentiation then rests on formula and brand, not manufacturing.

passages.title: Value Chain — FX exposure
passages.text: Every cross-geography number in this system is pinned to a single FX date (USD/KRW 1478.40, USD/INR 96.23, both 2026-07-21), and Korean retail figures are converted via the inverse of that rate. For an importer running the corridor, this is a real operating exposure, not just a modelling artefact: COGS accrue in KRW while MRP is set in INR, so KRW appreciation compresses the landed margin between purchase and sale. Any USD-normalised comparison across the two markets inherits the same single-date sensitivity. This is an inference from the pinned-rate structure, not an observed FX-loss datapoint.

passages.title: Corridor finding — competitive dynamics
passages.text: AmorePacific's India push predates the Nykaa-exclusive narrative and keeps broadening beyond it: the group entered India in 2013, has since added Reliance's Tira and Tata Cliq's Palette as further retail partners, and its India leadership describes a deliberately phased, 'test the market first' approach to adding brands rather than a full-portfolio rush. (Source: ETRetail (Economic Times Retail))

passages.title: Corridor finding — competitive dynamics
passages.text: Innisfree was the first Korean cosmetics brand to enter India, and did so via a wholly-owned 100% FDI structure rather than a franchise or local-distributor model — a comparatively capital-intensive entry mode for a first mover, per AmorePacific's then India managing director. (Source: ETBrandEquity (Economic Times))

passages.title: Corridor finding — competitive dynamics
passages.text: TirTir's India rollout was sequenced rather than simultaneous: it listed on Tira first (January 2025) and only added Nykaa about a year and a half later (June 2026), framing the Nykaa addition as reaching 'more local consumers' rather than replacing the first platform. (Source: The Korea Herald)

passages.title: Corridor finding — competitive dynamics
passages.text: Illiyoon's India launch sits inside a bigger corporate bet, not a one-off local SKU call: AmorePacific's November 2024 investor day named Illiyoon, alongside HERA and AESTURA, as one of its next-generation global growth brands, ahead of the India listing that followed. (Source: Amorepacific (Investor Day announcement))

passages.title: Corridor finding — competitive dynamics
passages.text: AmorePacific India's country head said in September 2025 that the group has plans to introduce more products in India and is open to eventually considering local manufacturing there — a longer-term ambition beyond the current platform/import model, though no plant has been announced. (Source: Livemint)

passages.title: Corridor finding — competitive dynamics
passages.text: Quench Botanics, an Indian skincare brand co-founded by actor Kareena Kapoor Khan, brings K-beauty-inspired formulations to India with an explicit mission to adapt ingredients and the multi-step Korean routine for Indian skin and climate — another India-side challenger alongside Pilgrim and Limese. (Source: t2ONLINE)

passages.title: Corridor finding — competitive dynamics
passages.text: Put Simply, an Indian skincare brand founded in 2022 after its founder's own acne struggles led him to Korean skincare, was built specifically as a range 'developed in Korea for Indian skin and weather' — part of a broader pattern of Indian founders sourcing formulation and manufacturing directly from Korea rather than only importing finished Korean brands. (Source: The Nod Mag)

passages.title: Corridor finding — competitive dynamics
passages.text: Industry commentary flags platform exclusivity as a coming fault line: as current exclusive agreements for global brands in India expire, quick-commerce players are expected to push for a share of those distribution rights — a dynamic to watch beyond today's Nykaa/Tira conduit split. (Source: LinkedIn (industry commentary))

passages.title: Corridor finding — consumer behaviour
passages.text: Tier-2/3 and non-metro India are already meaningful K-beauty demand centres, not just a future opportunity: cities like Guwahati and Lucknow show up as substantial contributors to tier-2 sales, with face care the largest category share, and e-commerce platforms report their heaviest non-metro demand from India's northeastern states, where K-pop and Korean-drama fandom runs deepest. (Source: Credence Research)

passages.title: Corridor finding — consumer behaviour
passages.text: South India is the fastest-growing K-beauty region, led by Bengaluru and Chennai's digitally-fluent tech-sector consumers and students; the regional preference skews toward lightweight gel textures, SPF suited to tropical humidity, and serums that state their active ingredients and efficacy claims plainly rather than relying on generic 'glow' marketing. (Source: Expert Market Research)

passages.title: Corridor finding — consumer behaviour
passages.text: Northeastern India's Korean-culture affinity goes beyond single-product trial: Innisfree India's own marketing manager describes the region as following the brand's full 10-step Korean skincare routine, not just buying hero SKUs piecemeal. (Source: ETBrandEquity (Economic Times))

passages.title: Corridor finding — consumer behaviour
passages.text: Innisfree India's leadership attributes early demand to a broader shift in Indian consumer preference toward natural, chemical-free products — positioning Korean brands as beneficiaries of that shift rather than the ones driving it. (Source: ETBrandEquity (Economic Times))

passages.title: Corridor finding — consumer behaviour
passages.text: A broader shift in the Indian beauty aesthetic itself — away from sharp contouring, bold brows and strong lip definition, toward a softer 'natural look' — is cited as an underlying tailwind that makes Korean product philosophy land well with Indian consumers. (Source: Maekyung Pulse)

passages.title: Corridor finding — consumer behaviour
passages.text: Price sensitivity, product complexity, and authenticity/counterfeit worries are the most-cited friction points slowing K-beauty adoption in India, even though a large majority of existing users say they intend to use more Korean products and are willing to pay a premium once quality is verified. (Source: ETRetail (citing Kindlife/Datum Intelligence))

passages.title: Corridor finding — consumer behaviour
passages.text: Newer science-led entrants are courting Indian consumers on specific, clinically-framed concerns — pigmentation, uneven skin texture, long-term skin health — rather than generic glow/glass-skin messaging; Dr. Melaxin's India launch messaging leans explicitly on this clinically-backed positioning. (Source: The Economic Times)

passages.title: Corridor finding — brand strategy
passages.text: Korean brands' 'herbal ingredient plus modern science' storytelling maps directly onto India's own pre-existing ayurvedic/herbal beliefs — Belif's chickweed, oat and celandine-based formulations are described as landing with Indian consumers precisely because India already has a deep cultural frame for herbal skincare, so the brand doesn't have to build that association from scratch. (Source: imnidhi.com)

passages.title: Corridor finding — brand strategy
passages.text: Early Korean entrants used hands-on brand education as a market-entry tactic rather than relying on paid media alone: The Face Shop flew Nykaa's team to Korea to tour its labs and brief its experts, specifically so Nykaa could produce more informed ingredient and innovation content for Indian shoppers; Nykaa credited the resulting brand launches with lifting its skin-care sales, and said digital was the only channel it was betting on to market them. (Source: ETBrandEquity (Economic Times))

passages.title: Corridor finding — brand strategy
passages.text: India-facing product write-ups frame Korean SKUs around local climate and skin fit rather than generic global claims: Sulwhasoo is positioned against pollution- and stress-dulled skin, Innisfree's Green Tea Seed Serum is framed for humid climates, COSRX and Some By Mi are aimed at oily/acne-prone skin, and Dr. Jart+ and Aestura are framed as fragrance-free options for sensitive skin — a consistent India-specific-fit narrative across otherwise-unrelated brands. (Source: Smytten)

passages.title: Corridor finding — brand strategy
passages.text: Nykaa's own messaging positions the retailer as having 'catalysed the K-beauty phenomenon' in India rather than simply stocking a trend it discovered — its Illiyoon launch communications lean on the decade-long AmorePacific relationship as the origin story of Korean beauty retail in the country. (Source: medianews4u.com)

passages.title: Corridor finding — brand strategy
passages.text: Flipkart's entry messaging is explicitly mass-access rather than curated-exclusive: it frames its Korean-brand storefront as 'democratising access' to K-beauty rituals 'at accessible price points' for digitally-native shoppers — a different position from Nykaa's and Tira's exclusive-brand curation approach. (Source: Flipkart (LinkedIn))

passages.title: Corridor finding — brand strategy
passages.text: AmorePacific's global 'Everyone Global' strategic pillar commits to developing region-localised product variants rather than exporting a single global catalogue, and names India explicitly as one of the key markets this localisation push covers. (Source: Personal Care Insights)

passages.title: Corridor finding — brand strategy
passages.text: Tira's brand messaging for each new Korean exclusive (Hince, Medicube, Dr. Melaxin) follows a consistent house style — 'globally coveted' / 'science-led' partnership language plus an omnichannel 'discovery to delivery' framing — regardless of how the underlying brand positions itself elsewhere. (Source: Reliance Industries Limited)

passages.title: Corridor finding — channel behaviour
passages.text: Zepto's own team frames its move into Korean-beauty listings as a deliberate widening from daily essentials to make-up to K-beauty specifically, reframing q-commerce beauty as convenience-driven rather than only last-minute or need-based shopping. (Source: The Established)

passages.title: Corridor finding — channel behaviour
passages.text: Blinkit's beauty push includes direct brand-partner tie-ups — for example with Etude — for quick delivery, rather than only passively listing SKUs sourced through distributors; this is a materially different channel relationship from a marketplace listing. (Source: NextLeap (Blinkit vs Zepto product teardown))

passages.title: Corridor finding — channel behaviour
passages.text: Zepto's own dedicated 'Korean Beauty Skincare Range' storefront returned zero live products when checked — a platform-specific whitespace signal that parallels the thin indie/derma K-brand stocking already seen on Blinkit, suggesting the gap isn't limited to one platform. (Source: Zepto)

passages.title: Corridor finding — channel behaviour
passages.text: Even where dark-store stocking is thin, marketplace demand signals for the same brands show up elsewhere: COSRX's Advanced Snail 96 Mucin Power Essence carries a six-figure rating count and a fast-moving 'bought in past week' flag on Amazon India, indicating real bestseller traction on marketplace channels even where q-commerce stocking lags. (Source: Amazon.in)

passages.title: Corridor finding — channel behaviour
passages.text: Beauty of Joseon's Relief Sunscreen is being actively marketed as a viral bestseller through Nykaa's own Instagram content pairing it with make-up products, and through independent Indian creator content — a concrete demand proof point behind sunscreen as a stand-out K-beauty sub-category in India. (Source: Nykaa (Instagram))

passages.title: Corridor finding — channel behaviour
passages.text: Tira's own positioning leans on deep, pincode-level delivery reach across India as its stated differentiator, framing itself as the access point that brings international brand launches to non-metro India rather than a metro-first premium platform. (Source: Reliance Industries Limited)

passages.title: Corridor finding — regulatory colour
passages.text: A CDSCO cosmetics Import Registration Certificate, once granted, is valid for three years from issuance (subject to earlier suspension or cancellation) — a renewal cadence importers need to plan around beyond the initial COS-1 to COS-2 application. (Source: CDSCO (Frequently Asked Questions on Registration and Import of Cosmetics))

passages.title: Corridor finding — regulatory colour
passages.text: CDSCO's own targeted processing window for import-registration applications is 90 days, but the underlying rules allow up to six months, extendable by a further three months in exceptional, recorded circumstances — a wide potential lead-time band for K-beauty entrants to plan launch timing around. (Source: CDSCO (Frequently Asked Questions on Registration and Import of Cosmetics))

passages.title: Corridor finding — regulatory colour
passages.text: Imported cosmetics face an animal-testing compliance step at the port that is separate from upfront registration: under Rule 135B, the manufacturer must give a written undertaking that the product was not tested on animals on or after 12 November 2014, submitted at the time of consignment clearance. (Source: CDSCO (Frequently Asked Questions on Registration and Import of Cosmetics))

passages.title: Corridor finding — regulatory colour
passages.text: A narrow carve-out exists for cosmetics imported in bulk purely for repackaging and 100% re-export: no Registration Certificate is required in that case, but the importer must separately obtain CDSCO HQ permission and give a written undertaking that the goods will not be released for domestic sale. (Source: CDSCO (Frequently Asked Questions on Registration and Import of Cosmetics))

passages.title: Corridor finding — regulatory colour
passages.text: FSSAI has separately flagged quick-commerce platforms for improper storage and handling practices covering cosmetics alongside food — a live compliance friction point for the q-commerce conduit that K-beauty distribution increasingly leans on for Tier 2/3 reach. (Source: NextLeap (Blinkit vs Zepto product teardown, citing FSSAI))

passages.title: Corridor finding — regulatory colour
passages.text: A Korean cosmetics manufacturer cannot import into India directly in its own name — it must appoint an Indian Authorised Agent (a locally established importer, subsidiary, or distributor) who holds the CDSCO registration and is legally answerable to the regulator, making that local entity the actual legal anchor point for compliance rather than the Korean manufacturer itself. (Source: Statura)

passages.title: India finding — supply chain
passages.text: Most Indian D2C beauty brands do NOT own factories — they use third-party contract manufacturers / private-label houses (e.g. Gorgeous Cosmos, and hundreds listed on IndiaMART), with MOQs from ~500 units. The brand owns formula/brand; the CM owns production. (Source: Gorgeous Cosmos; IndiaMART)

passages.title: India finding — supply chain
passages.text: FMCG brands demand audit-readiness/scale from CMs; D2C brands demand agility, small batches, and RM-sourcing transparency — two different contract-manufacturing service models. (Source: IMARC Engineering)

passages.title: India finding — supply chain
passages.text: Upstream, specialty-ingredient suppliers underpin the chain: Galaxy Surfactants (mild surfactants for cleansers) and Fine Organics (oleochemical specialty additives) are key Indian actives/ingredient makers. (Source: Marcellus; GlobalData)

passages.title: India finding — supply chain
passages.text: Speed-to-market is a distinct axis from customisation when choosing a manufacturing model: private-label routes (an existing formula sold under the client's brand) typically launch in 2-4 weeks, versus 4-8 weeks for full contract manufacturing with custom formulation — a tradeoff D2C founders weigh alongside MOQ when picking a manufacturing partner. (Source: Gorgeous Cosmos)

passages.title: India finding — supply chain
passages.text: India's D2C beauty 'moat' problem traces directly to its contract-manufacturing ecosystem: because hundreds of CMOs can replicate a similar formulation quickly and cheaply, brands that differentiate mainly through clean labels, packaging and a marketed 'hero' ingredient — rather than genuine formulation IP — look novel at launch but are easy for competitors to copy, leaving the underlying differentiation superficial. (Source: My PM Interview)

passages.title: India finding — import make
passages.text: India skincare is ~91% domestically supplied by value (imports ~US$844m vs ~US$9bn market); imports concentrate in premium and K-beauty tiers. Korea 17% and China 22% of skincare imports. (Source: UN Comtrade; IMARC (derived))

passages.title: India finding — import make
passages.text: Premium fragrance is import-reliant: UAE is India's largest perfume-import source (HS 3303), then France/Germany for high-end oils; mass perfume/deodorant is domestically filled. (Source: Seair Exim)

passages.title: India finding — import make
passages.text: Any imported cosmetic needs a CDSCO Import Registration (Form COS-1 -> COS-2 via SUGAM), plus manufacturing-site registration — the key lead-time/friction cost for K-beauty entrants. (Source: PSR Compliance / CDSCO)

passages.title: India finding — pricing
passages.text: India's skincare market stratifies into five price tiers with distinct competitive archetypes rather than a single mass-to-premium continuum: legacy FMCG brands (Pond's, Nivea, Himalaya, Lakme, Garnier) dominate the sub-Rs200 mass tier through deep offline distribution, while D2C-first brands (Minimalist, Dot & Key, Plum, Foxtale, Pilgrim, mCaffeine) cluster in the Rs500-1,500 mid-premium band that is both online-led and the fastest-growing tier below premium. (Source: IMA Pro)

passages.title: India finding — pricing
passages.text: Beauty's D2C unit economics are unusually forgiving relative to other Indian D2C categories — a serum costing Rs80-120 to manufacture typically sells for Rs500-700, leaving 55-70% true gross margin after packaging, shipping, returns and payment-gateway costs — which is cited as why acquirers can justify rich multiples (e.g. HUL's Minimalist deal) and why beauty D2C brands can sustain unusually heavy marketing spend relative to categories like food or fashion. (Source: The D2C Pulse)

passages.title: India finding — growth
passages.text: India's leading men's grooming D2C brands are sequencing international expansion around brand-building before volume: Beardo opened a flagship store in Sydney as a market statement rather than a soft test, and The Man Company built retail presence across the UAE, Southeast Asia and Western markets via Amazon Global and Nykaa Global — using low-commitment marketplace listings to earn the right to invest in higher-commitment physical presence, not the reverse. (Source: HavStrategy)

passages.title: India finding — growth
passages.text: In hair care, natural/organic formulations are called out as growing faster than the category overall while still holding a minority share — read as a sign that credible, ingredient-transparent natural formulation (not just a 'natural' label claim) still has early-mover room, because India's research-heavy D2C buyers actively check ingredient substantiation rather than reward badge-washing. (Source: Arise Cosmetic)

passages.title: India finding — new players
passages.text: Consolidation by strategics: HUL acquired Minimalist (~Rs3,000cr) and Plum; Estee Lauder took Forest Essentials; Puig bought 85% of Kama Ayurveda; KKR owns 54% of Vini Cosmetics/Fogg (US$625m, US$1.2bn valuation). (Source: IMA Pro; Economic Times)

passages.title: India finding — new players
passages.text: Funding continues into 2026 despite the broader D2C slowdown: KOSE invested US$30m in Foxtale, Moxie raised US$15m, Antinorm Rs28cr seed; India D2C attracted ~US$757m over 18 months (wellness+beauty led). (Source: The D2C Pulse; The Hindu BusinessLine)

passages.title: India finding — new players
passages.text: House-of-brands model emerging among small players: Innovist runs Bare Anatomy (hair), Chemist at Play (skin), Sunscoop (sun) as science-backed sub-brands. (Source: Indian Startup Times)

passages.title: India finding — new players
passages.text: K-beauty brand owners are entering directly: APR launched Medicube on Nykaa; AmorePacific introduced dermocosmetic brand Illiyoon — accelerating India entry to offset SWANA-region volatility. (Source: Personal Care Insights)

passages.title: India finding — new players
passages.text: The HUL-Minimalist acquisition mirrors a global strategic pattern rather than an India-specific one: Shiseido's acquisition of Dr. Dennis Gross Skincare and Estee Lauder's acquisition of DECIEM follow the same logic — legacy beauty majors buying efficacy-led, ingredient-forward challenger brands to upgrade into higher-growth, 'results-first' skincare rather than building that credibility organically. (Source: Future Market Insights)

passages.title: India finding — new players
passages.text: A parallel, less-visible consolidation wave is running through dermocosmetics specifically, led by pharma and pharma-adjacent acquirers rather than the FMCG/luxury strategics behind the marquee deals: Torrent Pharmaceuticals acquired derma player Curatio, Eris Lifesciences acquired nine cosmetic derma brands from Dr Reddy's and nine clinical derma brands from Glenmark, Encube acquired the commercial rights to Soframycin, and HUL separately acquired VWash to enter female intimate hygiene. (Source: KPMG)

passages.title: India finding — new players
passages.text: New Indian fragrance launches increasingly lead with culturally-blended, founder- or celebrity-led storytelling rather than pure Western positioning: actress Rashmika Mandanna's 'Dear Diary' blends Indian ingredients (jasmine, pink lotus) with global-style scent construction, and Fraganta's 'Ganga' and 'Jogi' scents are built explicitly around Indian cultural references. (Source: Renub Research)

passages.title: India finding — demand
passages.text: Beauty is one of the fastest-rising quick-commerce categories: ~160% YoY growth (RedSeer); premium/high-end beauty is gaining on q-commerce, not just mass. (Source: RedSeer (via Unicommerce))

passages.title: India finding — demand
passages.text: Q-commerce is ~Rs40,000cr (~US$5bn) GMV in 2026; share roughly Blinkit 45-50%, Zepto 20-25%, Instamart 20-25% — the new default access rail into Tier 2/3. (Source: Digital in Asia; Product Growth)

passages.title: India finding — demand
passages.text: Demand is shifting from awareness-led to access-led, driven by Gen Z, rising incomes, and vernacular/omnichannel reach; beauty has become a daily self-care essential, not aspirational luxury. (Source: Outlook Business (RedSeer))

passages.title: India finding — demand
passages.text: 'Skinification' is reshaping hair care (~US$4bn market): buyers want actives (niacinamide, ceramides, peptides) in serums/tonics; specialist D2C brands outperform legacy FMCG. (Source: Entrepreneur India; Arise)

passages.title: India finding — demand
passages.text: India's three leading quick-commerce platforms compete on structurally different axes rather than just discounting for the same share: Blinkit leads decisively on gross order value and skews toward established FMCG and high-frequency replenishment SKUs, Zepto is the most aggressive at onboarding new categories such as beauty, and Swiggy Instamart's relative strength is concentrated in South Indian metros. (Source: Global Ecommerce Solutions)

passages.title: India finding — demand
passages.text: In crowded, long-tail q-commerce categories like sunscreen, paid search visibility inside the app — not shelf space or brand loyalty — is described as the primary lever determining which brands actually get bought, since agile brands that react fastest to search trends and inventory gaps outmanoeuvre slower incumbents. (Source: LinkedIn (Samiran Mathur))

passages.title: India finding — demand
passages.text: Men's grooming demand growth is outrunning product depth in at least one sub-category: despite most Indian men preferring facial hair, beard care remains underdeveloped due to limited product innovation, and age-specific formulations are largely missing even as rising dry-skin complaints signal unmet demand for targeted men's skincare. (Source: Mintel)

passages.title: South Korea finding — supply chain
passages.text: Korea's ODM manufacturers (Cosmax, Kolmar Korea, Cosmecca and the wider ecosystem) function as manufacturing platforms that let an entrepreneur launch a brand without owning a factory or holding chemistry expertise -- an indie brand like Beauty of Joseon 'doesn't invent new molecules,' it sources formulation from the ODM and puts its own resources into trend identification, ingredient storytelling and packaging design instead. (Source: Georgetown Journal of International Affairs (Munseob Lee))

passages.title: South Korea finding — supply chain
passages.text: Korean ODMs can take a product from concept to shelf in under six months, versus years for a legacy Western brand, and now accept batches as small as 1,000 units -- collapsing the minimum-scale requirement that used to gate entry, and letting ODM-scale economies deliver what the author calls 'masstige' (prestige-grade quality at mass prices) for a brand that owns no manufacturing of its own. (Source: Georgetown Journal of International Affairs (Munseob Lee))

passages.title: South Korea finding — supply chain
passages.text: Sharing the same K-beauty demand boom does not guarantee the same profitability for Korea's big ODMs: Kolmar Korea posted a record operating margin as profit grew faster than revenue, while Cosmax's revenue grew faster than its operating profit, because newer clients tend to bring smaller, more frequent orders that run less efficiently for the manufacturer -- the same order-book growth can read as strength or as margin dilution depending on customer mix. (Source: Korea Biomedical Review)

passages.title: South Korea finding — supply chain
passages.text: Cosmecca Korea's growth was unusually lopsided by geography: both revenue and profit grew fastest among the big three ODMs on the strength of domestic Korean skincare demand and its U.S. operations, even as its China business contracted -- a sign that ODM fortunes are now tracking the same US/Europe pivot reshaping Korean brand exports, not China. (Source: Korea Biomedical Review)

passages.title: South Korea finding — channels
passages.text: Olive Young controls more than 85% of South Korea's health-and-beauty store market through over 1,380 stores nationwide -- a concentration high enough that, because it controls where Korean consumers discover skincare, the retailer effectively decides which brands get shelf-driven scale and which stay niche; the piece describes it as having become 'less a store and more a kingmaker.' (Source: Seoulz)

passages.title: South Korea finding — channels
passages.text: Olive Young's home-market dominance gives it leverage over the entire supply chain, functioning less like a retailer and more like an incubator that spots hits via real-time merchandising data -- a moat strong enough that Sephora and Ulta reportedly raced to lock up exclusive deals with major Korean brands specifically to blunt Olive Young's own overseas expansion. (Source: Seoulz)

passages.title: South Korea finding — channels
passages.text: Korea's beauty retail has structurally flipped from offline- to online-led in five years: e-commerce's share of Korea's cosmetics market rose from 39.1% in 2019 to 60.8% in 2024, with offline's share falling by the same margin in reverse -- a reversal significant enough that even legacy luxury houses (Chanel, Prada and Nars among those named) are now expanding onto Korean e-commerce platforms rather than staying department-store-first. (Source: Korea JoongAng Daily)

passages.title: South Korea finding — channels
passages.text: Luxury beauty brands frame their Korean e-commerce push as defensive as much as opportunistic: one industry source ties it directly to K-beauty's domestic rise, saying the category's growth 'has weakened brand loyalty toward overseas beauty brands, particularly among consumers in their 20s and 30s, making it necessary to secure new sales channels,' while a global beauty brand representative separately values Korea as a testing ground because 'consumers respond quickly to new products.' (Source: Korea JoongAng Daily)

passages.title: South Korea finding — channels
passages.text: Live commerce has become a distinct beauty-specific channel layered on top of e-commerce and Olive Young: hosts demonstrate texture and application on camera and answer viewer questions in real time, which the format's proponents say resolves a shopper 'confidence gap' that static product pages can't -- and a live broadcast specifically on Olive Young is treated as a credibility signal ('shelf-placement legitimacy') for a foreign brand, not just a sales event. (Source: Seoulz)

passages.title: South Korea finding — channels
passages.text: The Chinese daigou (bulk-reseller) channel that once anchored Korean duty-free cosmetics sales is a genuinely distinct channel from domestic retail, and its decline has three compounding causes rather than one: younger Chinese travelers have shifted to independent travel and moved past a 'duty free equals bargain equals must-buy' mindset; the same Korean goods are now buyable on Chinese e-commerce or in China's own expanding duty-free zones (including a new island-wide zone on Hainan); and Beijing has directly cracked down on the daigou trade itself while expanding domestic alternatives to it. (Source: The Korea Times)

passages.title: South Korea finding — channels
passages.text: Duty-free's daigou channel is volatile and margin-driven rather than in simple one-way decline: Lotte Duty Free halted sales to Chinese bulk resellers in January 2025 to protect margins, then reversed course five months later once overall sales suffered and rival operators Shilla and Shinsegae kept serving daigou anyway -- Lotte now frames its return as selective, doing daigou deals 'only when profitability is assured' rather than chasing volume the way it did pre-pandemic, when daigou made up roughly half of duty-free sales. (Source: KED Global)

passages.title: South Korea finding — competitive structure
passages.text: AmorePacific and LG H&H's long-standing domestic duopoly is being challenged from below: both conglomerates have 'ceded market leadership' in growth terms to fast-rising challengers APR (Medicube's parent) and Goodai Global, and industry commentary now frames K-beauty's global success as defined by 'a growing number of smaller companies with competitive brands' rather than by the two incumbents. (Source: The Korea Times)

passages.title: South Korea finding — competitive structure
passages.text: Both incumbents are responding to indie-brand pressure by shedding non-cosmetics assets to refocus capital: AmorePacific is selling its Anseong health-supplement plant to 'manage our assets more efficiently,' and LG H&H is divesting its Haitai HTB beverage subsidiary to 'restructure our strategic portfolio' -- both moves read as freeing up capital to acquire indie brands and reinvest in cosmetics rather than raising cash for its own sake. (Source: The Korea Times)

passages.title: South Korea finding — competitive structure
passages.text: APR's rise past LG H&H (and its narrowing gap with AmorePacific) is attributed to structural agility rather than scale: its outsourced-manufacturing model supports small launches that pivot quickly to social-media-driven trends, and its e-commerce-first approach caught the US online shift that AmorePacific and LG H&H -- both historically offline-channel-heavy -- were slow to move on; legacy conglomerates are also described as carrying higher minimum production runs and being slower to discontinue underperforming products because of sunk costs. (Source: KED Global)

passages.title: South Korea finding — competitive structure
passages.text: The conglomerates have swapped the domestic #1 spot before: LG H&H overtook AmorePacific during the pandemic because its non-beauty product spread (toothpaste, detergent) buffered the shock, while AmorePacific's heavier reliance on physical stores and foreign-tourist footfall left it exposed -- it closed 661 brand stores between late 2018 and mid-2020 -- and LG H&H additionally out-executed AmorePacific in China's Singles' Day luxury sales over the same period, a precedent for how quickly relative position can shift when a channel or region turns. (Source: The Korea Herald)

passages.title: South Korea finding — competitive structure
passages.text: AmorePacific's own leadership frames its response to indie competition as deliberately not racing indie brands to shelf speed: its CEO is quoted questioning indie sustainability ('they are sometimes only a few months old') and the company is described as playing a patient '10-year strategy' -- leaning on 400+ in-house researchers, owned ingredient farms, dermacosmetics retail education, and international expansion (17 European countries, Amazon) rather than competing on launch speed. (Source: BeautyMatter (Janna Mandell))

passages.title: South Korea finding — demand drivers
passages.text: Domestic Korean skincare demand is shifting toward 'medical ingredient' skincare -- actives like PDRN, exosomes and tranexamic acid that read as clinically proven and dermatologist-trusted are mainstreaming -- alongside a stated expectation that efficacy alone is no longer enough: brands are also expected to deliver a distinctive sensory user experience, not just results. (Source: BeautyMatter (Janna Mandell))

passages.title: South Korea finding — demand drivers
passages.text: Korean beauty demand is blurring category lines in two directions at once: colour cosmetics (CC creams, concealers, tinted moisturizers) are being reformulated with active skincare ingredients so makeup does double duty as treatment, while skincare-style actives and routines are simultaneously migrating into hair and scalp care -- extending 'skinification' logic across categories rather than keeping it confined to the face. (Source: BeautyMatter (Janna Mandell))

passages.title: South Korea finding — demand drivers
passages.text: Alongside efficacy, Korean consumers are described as wanting products with 'playful cute design,' collectible packaging and a joyful brand experience, plus -- as a climate-linked trend -- formulations that deliver an immediate cooling sensation on the skin, signalling that functional/clinical positioning and playful sensory design are both live demand levers at once, not substitutes for each other. (Source: BeautyMatter (Janna Mandell))

passages.title: South Korea finding — export orientation
passages.text: Korea's cosmetics export mix flipped in 2025: the United States became Korea's largest cosmetics export market for the first time, overtaking China (long the dominant destination), while exports to Europe were accelerating even faster through early 2026 -- a geographic reorientation an industry analyst expects to put Europe in the lead export-market position by the end of 2026. These are export figures specifically and should not be read as Korea's domestic retail size. (Source: Korea JoongAng Daily)

passages.title: South Korea finding — export orientation
passages.text: Indie brands (APR, d'Alba, Beauty of Joseon, Anua and SKIN1004 among those named) are described as the engine of this export pivot, going direct to Western consumers via Amazon, TikTok Shop and other digital platforms rather than the department-store and offline-retail relationships the conglomerates built their earlier export era on -- the same social-first, e-commerce-first playbook pressuring the conglomerates at home is what's winning them share abroad. (Source: Korea JoongAng Daily)

passages.title: South Korea finding — export orientation
passages.text: A Korea Federation of Small and Medium Business survey of roughly 1,300 firms found strong majorities of both cosmetics and bio/medical firms positive on 2026 export prospects, citing new product launches, quality gains, market diversification and favourable exchange rates as growth drivers -- but firms flagged China's low-price competitive strategy and tariff uncertainty as live headwinds, and are asking government for expanded export vouchers, tariff diplomacy and help with foreign regulatory compliance. (Source: The Korea Herald)

passages.title: Corridor — trade_base
passages.text: ~US$50m (H1 2025 basis), +44.7% YoY — small base, fast growth

passages.title: Corridor — momentum
passages.text: K-beauty is accelerating its India entry to offset SWANA-region volatility (Personal Care Insights, Apr 2026). 2026 launches: APR's Medicube (Nykaa + Tira), AmorePacific's Illiyoon (Nykaa exclusive), TirTir (Nykaa, Jun 2026), Tira's Hince (Jan) and Dr. Melaxin (Jul). India K-beauty ~INR 3,139cr (2025) forecast ~26% CAGR to ~INR 32,424cr by 2035 (Expert Market Research). AmorePacific is scaling India via platforms/imports, NOT local manufacturing — no India plant announced.

passages.text: Mid-price derma K-beauty in Tier 2/3 (baseline whitespace #5, highest corridor conviction)

passages.title: Q-commerce assortment insight
passages.text: Conglomerate-owned K-brands (AmorePacific, LG H&H) have mature India supply chains and are deeply stocked on q-commerce; the viral indie/derma brands driving the K-beauty narrative (COSRX, Anua, Some By Mi) are out-of-stock, 'coming soon', or absent. The real Tier 2/3 whitespace is getting indie derma K-beauty onto the q-commerce rail, not the conglomerate brands already there.

passages.text: Primary conduit; 10-year AmorePacific partnership (2016-2026), India's largest Korean portfolio (skincare/derma/haircare). Illiyoon newest exclusive (2026). Now also carries non-AmorePacific K-brands (TirTir, Medicube). Brands carried: Innisfree, Laneige, Sulwhasoo, COSRX, Aestura, Illiyoon, Mise En Scène, RYO, TirTir, Medicube
